title: Garner is still the floor: a Tulsa shooting goes to a jury, Barnes v. Felix ends, and body camera footage becomes a two-way street
summary: A corrective week after a spring of Supreme Court decisions that broadened merits review and narrowed qualified immunity. In Manning v. City of Tulsa, a published Tenth Circuit opinion filed March 30, the court denied qualified immunity to former Tulsa officer Betty Shelby in the September 2016 shooting of Terrence Crutcher, holding that Tennessee v. Garner, a Supreme Court deadly force decision squarely on point, put the unlawfulness of shooting an unarmed, non-dangerous subject beyond debate without any further specificity. The case now goes to a jury. On April 27 the Supreme Court denied certiorari a second time in Barnes v. Felix, ending that case with the officer winning under the totality framework the Court itself announced a year earlier. And on April 9 the Colorado Court of Appeals held that Boulder could not charge more than $8,000 for body camera footage of a fatal officer-involved shooting. Nothing from the Ninth Circuit and nothing from California in this episode.
coverage: The episode did not describe which courts or databases it swept for the week of May 11 to 16, 2026. It covered three items: the Tenth Circuit's Manning v. City of Tulsa opinion, the Supreme Court's second certiorari denial in Barnes v. Felix, and a Colorado Court of Appeals ruling on body camera fees. It reported nothing from the Ninth Circuit and nothing from California.

All three decisions predate the coverage window as the episode dated them: Manning was filed March 30, 2026, the Colorado decision was issued April 9, 2026, and the certiorari denial came April 27, 2026. The episode did not say when it learned of them or whether anything was filed during the week itself.

No docket numbers, panel compositions, or dissents were given for any item, and the episode did not say whether it read the opinions in full or worked from summaries. Case names and personal names are spelled as the machine transcript rendered them.
This brief was rebuilt from the episode originally published on May 16, 2026; it was not re-researched, so verify every citation against the opinion before relying on it.

sections.heading: Supreme Court
sections.note: No merits decision this week. The one Supreme Court item is the April 27 certiorari denial that ends Barnes v. Felix, covered in full in the May 9 brief. The short version: after the Court's unanimous May 2025 decision rejected the moment of threat rule and required a totality of the circumstances analysis, the Fifth Circuit on remand, on September 18, 2025, again granted Officer Felix qualified immunity because the whole encounter supported his perception of imminent danger, and the second petition was denied on April 27, 2026. The episode's reading is that doctrine and outcome are not the same thing: the same officer won on the same facts under both frameworks, so Barnes was a doctrinal shift, not a results shift. Officers whose pre-engagement record is sloppy will fare worse under totality than under moment of threat; officers whose record supports their perception will not. The episode framed the week against the spring term's qualified immunity decisions covered the week before, Smith v. Scott on the shadow docket and Zorn: merits review got broader, immunity got narrower, and the agency carried the practical compliance load. As the Tenth Circuit described them in Manning, Smith involved a behavioral health restraint where the prior precedent was lower court excessive force law, and Zorn involved a wrist lock where the prior precedent was a different circuit's pain compliance ruling. Neither reaches a deadly force shooting governed by Tennessee v. Garner.

cases.name: Manning v. City of Tulsa
cases.topic: Deadly force against an unarmed subject, qualified immunity, Garner as clearly established law
cases.caution: The episode gave no docket number, no panel composition, and did not say whether there was a dissent. It did not explain who the named plaintiff Manning is. The "big bad dude" quotation is the episode's rendering of the helicopter officer's narration. The spellings of Crutcher and Shelby follow the machine transcript. The episode called this the first major federal appellate decision since Smith v. Scott to deny qualified immunity in a deadly force case; that is its characterization, not a verified count. Verify against the slip opinion before quoting it.
cases.facts: On the night of September 16, 2016, Terrence Crutcher, a 40-year-old Black man, was driving home in North Tulsa when his SUV stalled in the road. He left the vehicle and was walking near it when officers responded to reports of an abandoned vehicle. Officer Betty Shelby arrived first; other officers joined within minutes, a police helicopter recorded from above, and a dash camera in a second cruiser was also recording. The video shows Crutcher walking away from Shelby toward his vehicle with his hands raised above his head, not moving aggressively and not advancing on any officer. The helicopter officer narrated that Crutcher looked like a "big bad dude" and might be on something. As Crutcher reached the driver's side window, Shelby fired one shot from about 15 feet away as another officer deployed a Taser. Crutcher collapsed and died at the scene. He was unarmed, there was no weapon in the vehicle, and he was not suspected of any crime. Shelby was charged with manslaughter and acquitted in 2017. In 2024 the district court granted her qualified immunity, holding that no clearly established law prohibited deadly force where, as Shelby described it, the officer perceived the subject reaching into a vehicle window for a possible weapon. The district court treated Shelby's perception as the determinative fact.
cases.holding: Reversed, in a published opinion filed March 30, 2026. The case now heads to a jury trial nearly ten years after the shooting. The Tenth Circuit held that the district court got the specificity inquiry wrong. The court did not need a prior case with identical facts; it needed a prior case that placed the unlawfulness of Shelby's conduct beyond debate at the level of generality the conduct actually presented. That case was Tennessee v. Garner, the Supreme Court's 1985 decision holding that an officer may not seize an unarmed, non-dangerous suspect by shooting him dead unless the suspect poses a threat of serious physical harm to the officer or others. Crutcher was unarmed, and a reasonable jury could find he was non-dangerous, particularly given the dash camera and helicopter footage showing him walking with his hands raised as he approached his vehicle. If a jury could find those facts, Garner placed the unlawfulness of the shooting beyond debate. The panel distinguished Smith v. Scott, a behavioral health restraint case where the prior precedent was lower court excessive force law, and Zorn, a wrist lock case where the prior precedent was a different circuit's pain compliance ruling. Here the prior precedent was a Supreme Court deadly force decision squarely on point, so no further specificity was required.
cases.notDecided: Whether Shelby in fact reasonably perceived a threat. The panel held only that a reasonable jury could reject her account on the video; her perception of threat remains the central question at trial.
cases.inPractice: The Garner floor is still the floor. Whatever the doctrinal complexity of Smith and Zorn, an officer may not use deadly force against an unarmed, non-dangerous subject, and that rule has been clearly established for forty years. The post-Smith narrowing of qualified immunity does not reach Garner-type facts. Video was decisive here: without the dash camera and helicopter footage, Shelby's subjective perception would have been the primary record of what happened, and with the video her perception became one piece of evidence among several. The helicopter officer's contemporaneous, recorded, and arguably racialized narration became part of the record the appellate court reviewed.
cases.trainIt: Teach deadly force authority on the Garner framework first, then layer on the post-Smith specificity inquiry. Train officers that under Barnes and the totality framework the universe of evidence about an encounter is getting larger, not smaller; body cameras, dash cameras, and helicopter footage are part of the agency's risk posture both for and against the officer. Train officers that whatever they say while a recording device is rolling will be heard by everyone who reviews the case, including what other officers in the encounter say, and train command staff and FTOs to coach officers out of language that makes a defense difficult. Finally, train officers to document their threat perception cleanly, in body camera narration, in the post-incident report, and in the threat assessment they articulate to dispatch and other officers. Officers whose stated perception is undermined by contemporaneous video lose that advantage.

cases.name: Boulder body camera fee ruling (Yellow Scene Magazine request)
cases.topic: Public access to body camera footage, agency fees in misconduct cases
cases.caution: The episode did not give the case caption, a docket number, the citation of the Colorado statute, or the publication status of the decision. The spelling of Jeanette Alatorre follows the machine transcript. The episode did not say whether the ruling is published.
cases.facts: Yellow Scene Magazine sought body camera footage from a December 2023 fatal officer-involved shooting in Boulder that killed a woman named Jeanette Alatorre. The City of Boulder demanded more than $8,000 to release the footage, and the case arose from that demand. Colorado has a statute requiring release of body camera evidence in officer-involved shooting cases, so the question was whether the city could condition release of that footage on a fee of that size. The episode described this as a smaller story than the two federal items, but one that quietly shifts the landscape for misconduct litigation across the country, because the fight over access to footage is part of how misconduct cases get built.
cases.holding: On April 9, 2026, the Colorado Court of Appeals ruled that the City of Boulder cannot charge fees for body camera footage related to police misconduct complaints. The court said the fee was inconsistent with Colorado's statute requiring release of body camera evidence in officer-involved shooting cases. The decision binds only Colorado, but the episode read it as a signal of a trend. Several states have passed laws over the past five years requiring release of body camera footage in misconduct cases, and courts are increasingly hostile to agency fee structures that effectively price journalists and plaintiffs out of access. The episode expects the trend to spread to other states and circuits.
cases.inPractice: Body camera footage in misconduct cases is going to be released, often quickly and at low cost. Agencies that have built budgets around fee revenue from public records requests should plan for that change. Footage that is missing because the camera was off, or that ends abruptly mid-incident, is going to be a litigation problem. And video that helps the officer becomes available on the same terms as video that hurts.
cases.trainIt: Review retention and access policies so they anticipate fast, low-cost release in misconduct cases. Tighten activation discipline: activate early, leave the camera on through the entire encounter, and narrate decisions in real time. Train officers to use body camera narration to document their threat perception, the alternatives they considered, the warnings they issued, and the medical monitoring they performed. Under Barnes and the totality framework, that real-time narration is high-quality evidence in the officer's favor when the encounter is otherwise difficult.

applications.title: Teach Garner first
applications.body: An officer may not use deadly force against an unarmed, non-dangerous subject, and that rule has been clearly established for forty years. Manning shows that the Smith and Zorn narrowing of qualified immunity does not reach Garner-type facts, so train deadly force authority on Garner and layer the specificity inquiry on top.

applications.title: The record is getting bigger, and so is what you say on it
applications.body: Dash camera and helicopter video turned the Tulsa officer's perception from the primary record into one piece of evidence among several, and a helicopter officer's remark that the subject looked like a big bad dude became part of the appellate record. Whatever is said while a camera is rolling will be heard by everyone who reviews the case.

applications.title: Document the threat perception
applications.body: The officer's stated perception of threat will be the central question at the Manning trial. Officers who document that perception cleanly, in body camera narration, in the report, and in what they tell dispatch and other officers, hold a meaningfully better defensive position than officers whose account is undermined by the video.

applications.title: Doctrine is not outcome
applications.body: Barnes broadened the analysis, and the same officer on the same facts still won on remand because the pre-engagement record supported his perception of danger. Do not let anyone sell a Supreme Court ruling as an overnight game changer, and do not assume totality review helps or hurts officers in general; it rewards agencies that do the tactical and documentation work and punishes those that do not.

applications.title: Body camera footage is a two-way street
applications.body: After the Colorado ruling, expect footage in misconduct cases to be released faster and cheaper. Activate early, stay on through the whole encounter, and narrate warnings, alternatives, and medical monitoring in real time, because the same footage that supports a plaintiff can support the officer's defense.

applications.title: Walk the strip mall hypothetical
applications.body: An unarmed, non-aggressive man near parked cars who is not responding to commands and may be intoxicated or in crisis, with body camera and dash camera rolling and a second officer staged 30 feet away. After Barnes the court looks at tactics, de-escalation, cover, distance, and resources called for; after Manning the Garner floor applies no matter how the encounter feels. The right answer is still distance, communication, patience, and resources.

quiz.q: In Manning v. City of Tulsa, why did the Tenth Circuit deny qualified immunity even after the Supreme Court's recent specificity decisions?
options: Because the officer was acquitted of manslaughter, which settled the civil case
Because Tennessee v. Garner, a Supreme Court deadly force decision squarely on point, put the unlawfulness of shooting an unarmed, non-dangerous subject beyond debate
Because the helicopter officer's narration proved the shooting was unreasonable
Because qualified immunity no longer applies to deadly force cases
quiz.teach: The court did not need a prior case with identical facts, only one that placed the unlawfulness beyond debate at the level of generality the conduct presented. Garner, a Supreme Court holding on deadly force against an unarmed, non-dangerous subject, needed no further specificity, and the video let a reasonable jury find those facts.

quiz.q: What happened in Barnes v. Felix after the Supreme Court rejected the moment of threat rule in May 2025?
options: The Fifth Circuit found for the plaintiff and sent the case to trial
The Supreme Court decided the merits itself and ruled for the officer
The Fifth Circuit applied the totality framework, again granted the officer qualified immunity, and the Supreme Court denied a second certiorari petition on April 27, 2026
The case settled before the Fifth Circuit ruled
quiz.teach: The same officer won on the same facts under both frameworks because the pre-engagement record supported his perception of imminent danger. Barnes was a doctrinal shift, not a results shift, and totality review rewards sound tactics and clean documentation.

quiz.q: What did the Colorado Court of Appeals hold in the Boulder body camera case?
options: Agencies may charge any reasonable fee for body camera footage
Body camera footage of officer-involved shootings is exempt from public records laws

The city could not charge more than $8,000 for footage of a misconduct complaint because the fee was inconsistent with Colorado's statute requiring release of body camera evidence in officer-involved shootings
Journalists must obtain a court order before requesting footage
quiz.teach: The ruling binds only Colorado, but it signals a trend toward fast, low-cost release of footage in misconduct cases. Treat the camera as part of the official record: activate early, stay on, and narrate decisions in real time.
